clues: In the 15th century, medieval texts described this disease as being caused by old physical injuries that failed to heal properly. Some recommended treatments including wrapping the abdomen in warm linen or anointing the lower abdomen with hot honey, burnt stags' horns, and wood ashes.
You may have heard of Henrietta Lacks and her immortal cells. She had this disease and went to Johns Hopkins where samples were taken during treatment and ultimately became the HeLa cell line
One of the few human cancers that is almost entirely preventable through vaccination and regular screening, rates of this disease dropped over the past few decades.

President Eisenhower suffered from years of abdominal pain and was diagnosed with this disease first by an x-ray series and then later confirmed when he underwent emergency surgery for a small bowel obstruction. He recovered and won his re-election as president of the United States the next year.
King Alfred the Great (849-900AD) is also thought to have suffered from this disease with painful debilitating episodes of abdominal pain, peri-anal lesions, and diarrhea

The first recorded description of this disease may have been by Greek physician Aretaeus of Cappadocia in the 1st century although it was not formally identified and named until 1932 when an American Gastroenterologist published a landmark paper describing a disease of the terminal ileum affecting mainly young adults

In 1835, French and Belgian chemists isolated phlorizin from the root bark of apple trees, which blocked transporters in the intestines and kidneys leading to severe diarrhea, cramping, and malabsorption. Switching from an oxygen atom to a carbon atom allowed for this more selective class of medications to be developed.

These medications block sodium and glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule which leads to constriction of the afferent arteriole, reducing stress on the glomeruli and slowing the progression of chronic kidney disease
This class of medications can also reduce heart failure hospitalizations but the glucosuria can cause euglycemic DKA and increase the risk of UTIs.

This medication was discovered and developed at the Merck Frosst research hub located in a suburb of Montreal, Canada. By the time its patent expired in 2012, this was Merck's top-selling product, generating roughly $5 billion a year in sales

Part of the name of this medication is actually from the location it was discovered. Although this medication was approved by the FDA in 1998, after years of consumer advocacy and post-market tracking, the FDA attached a Black Box Warning in 2020 to notify patients of potential neuropsychiatric risks including vivid nightmares, depression, and suicidal thoughts.

In 1930, researchers found an unknown substance in the sputum of asthmatics and named it the 'Slow-Reacting Substance of Anaphylaxis'. It wasn't until the 70s and 80s that scienties figured out these were a group of inflammatory chemicals called leukotrienes. This medication was the first highly effective drug to block those molecules.

The first descriptions of this disease came from Guillaume de Baillou in 1578 where he described: 'symptoms are severe. The lung is so irritated that, at every attempt to expel the cause of his distress, he can neither inhale nor exhale. The sufferer seems to swell up and, as if about to strangle himself, holds his breath'

In the 1930s in Michigan, two female scientists, Pearl Kendrick and Grace Eldering, started research into this disease in their free time after work. They mixed their own specialized agar plates and asked sick children to cough on each plate to collect the causal bacteria, which allowed them to develop a potent whole-cell vaccine

Some individuals affected by this disease develop a characteristic high-pitched gasping sound after a coughing fit, but babies might become apneic instead. The vaccine is recommended starting from the age of 2 months and protects against this disease as well as two others.
